hand/logarithmic-geometry.html:
Log Riemann–Hilbert Correspondence and Irregular Connections

The classical Riemann–Hilbert correspondence identifies regular holonomic D‑modules on a smooth complex variety with perverse sheaves on the associated analytic space. In logarithmic geometry the correspondence extends to meromorphic connections with logarithmic poles along a normal crossing divisor. Kato and Nakayama constructed a topological space Xlog that captures the monodromy of such connections; the log de Rham complex Ω•X(log) computes the cohomology of the corresponding local system on Xlog. For irregular connections the Stokes phenomenon appears, and the logarithmic enhancement of the irregular Riemann–Hilbert correspondence (Mochizuki, Kedlaya) replaces the usual Stokes filtration by a log‑Stokes filtration on the log de Rham complex. The key object is the log irregular holonomic D‑module, whose solutions form a constructible complex on the Kato–Nakayama space with a prescribed growth condition at the boundary. The equivalence of categories is proved by combining the log de Rham functor with the log Stokes functor, and it respects the six operations (pushforward, pullback, tensor, dual) in the log setting. This framework underlies the geometric Langlands program for curves with ramification, where the Hecke eigensheaves are realized as log D‑modules with prescribed irregular singularities.

Log Prismatic Cohomology and the Breuil–Kisin Classification

Prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, provides a universal p‑adic cohomology theory for formal schemes. When a log structure is present, one works with log prisms (A, I, M) where M is a monoid mapping to A and the ideal I is equipped with a divided power structure compatible with the log structure. The log prismatic site (X, MX)△ yields a cohomology theory H•△(X, MX) that specializes to log crystalline cohomology after base change to the Breuil–Kisin prism and to log étale cohomology after inverting p. The Breuil–Kisin classification of finite flat group schemes over a p‑adic DVR extends to log group schemes: a log finite flat group scheme over (R, MR) corresponds to a log Breuil–Kisin module, i.e. a finite free module over the log Breuil–Kisin ring equipped with a Frobenius semilinear map and a log monodromy operator N satisfying the usual compatibility. The log prismatic F‑gauge (Fil•, φ) encodes the Hodge–Tate weights of the associated Galois representation, and the log Nygaard filtration gives the weight filtration predicted by the weight–monodromy conjecture. This theory has been used to prove the log version of the Fontaine–Mazur conjecture for varieties with semistable reduction, and it provides the p‑adic input for the Fargues–Scholze geometric Langlands correspondence on the log Fargues–Fontaine curve.

Worked Example: Computing Log Prismatic Cohomology of a Nodal Curve
Let X be a nodal cubic over a perfect field k of characteristic p > 0, equipped with the divisorial log structure given by the node. Compute H1△(X, MX) and identify its Hodge–Tate weights.
The log prismatic site of (X, MX) is equivalent to the prismatic site of the normalization X̃ together with a gluing datum at the two preimages of the node. The log prismatic cohomology fits into a Mayer–Vietoris sequence 0 → H0△(X) → H0△(X̃) ⊕ H0△(Spec k) → H0△(two points) → H1△(X) → H1△(X̃) → 0. Since X̃ ≅ ℙ1 has H1△(X̃) = 0, the map from the two points is surjective and H1△(X) ≅ k. The Hodge–Tate weights are obtained from the Nygaard filtration: Fil0 = H1△, Fil1 = 0, so the only weight is 0. This matches the expectation that the log H1 of a nodal curve is a Tate twist of the trivial representation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison between log crystalline and log prismatic cohomology, first state the base prisms (Breuil–Kisin vs. q‑de Rham) and then recall that both theories satisfy the same six functor formalism. The log Nygaard filtration is the bridge: its graded pieces give the log Hodge–Tate cohomology, which is canonically isomorphic to log de Rham cohomology. Write down the exact triangle relating the three cohomologies; examiners often award marks for citing the triangle rather than reproducing the full construction.

Log Perfectoid Spaces and the Fargues–Fontaine Curve

Perfectoid spaces, introduced by Scholze, admit a natural logarithmic enhancement: a log perfectoid space is a perfectoid space equipped with an fs log structure such that the tilt functor preserves the log structure. The log tilt (X♭, MX♭) is again a log perfectoid space, and the log Fontaine period map extends to a morphism of log diamonds. The Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF = (Y {∞})/φℤ carries a canonical log structure coming from the divisor at infinity; its log structure is fs and the associated Kato–Nakayama space is a circle bundle over the usual curve. Vector bundles on the log Fargues–Fontaine curve are classified by the log version of the Bhatt–Scholze theorem: they correspond to log Breuil–Kisin modules with a Frobenius and a monodromy operator satisfying the log Griffiths transversality condition. The log geometric Langlands correspondence of Fargues–Scholze uses the stack BunGlog of G‑bundles on the log curve; the Hecke operators act on the log étale cohomology of this stack, and the spectral side is given by log local systems on the log curve. The log structure is essential for handling ramified Langlands parameters, because the monodromy at the divisor encodes the Swan conductor of the corresponding Galois representation.

Log Motivic Homotopy Theory and the Logarithmic Six Functors

Voevodsky’s motivic homotopy theory has a logarithmic analogue developed by Binda, Park, and Østvær. The log motivic category DMlog(k) is built from log smooth schemes over a field k with the log Nisnevich topology; its objects are log motives Mlog(X) and the morphisms are given by log correspondences. The six functors (f!, f!, f*, f*, ⊗, Hom) exist on DMlog and satisfy the usual adjunctions and projection formulas, with the additional feature that the log purity isomorphism identifies the log motive of a log smooth pair (X, D) with a Tate twist of the log motive of the complement. The log motivic t‑structure yields a heart of log mixed motives, and the log étale realization functor lands in the derived category of log ℓ‑adic sheaves, compatible with the log weight filtration. The log motivic cohomology groups Hi,jmot(X, MX) compute higher Chow groups with log support, and they satisfy a log version of the Beilinson–Soulé vanishing conjecture. This theory provides the motivic input for the log version of the Bloch–Kato conjecture and for the construction of log motivic L‑functions.

Log Tropical Geometry, Mirror Symmetry, and Enumerative Invariants

Tropical geometry studies degenerations of algebraic varieties via piecewise‑linear objects. In the logarithmic setting, a log smooth morphism f: X → S with a standard log point base gives a tropicalization map trop: Xan → Σ(X/S) where Σ(X/S) is the cone complex of the log structure. The log Gromov–Witten invariants of a log Calabi–Yau pair (X, D) are defined by integrating against the virtual fundamental class on the moduli stack of log stable maps; they coincide with the usual Gromov–Witten invariants when D is empty. The log mirror symmetry conjecture (Gross–Siebert) asserts that the scattering diagram constructed from the log tropical data of a mirror pair reproduces the log Gromov–Witten invariants via the broken line algorithm. The log tropical vertex formalism computes these invariants combinatorially, and the log theta functions provide a basis of the log coordinate ring of the mirror. Recent work of Abramovich–Chen–Gross–Siebert extends the correspondence to higher genus and to log stable maps with arbitrary contact orders, using the log obstruction theory of the moduli space. These enumerative invariants are expected to satisfy the log version of the holomorphic anomaly equation and to be governed by a log topological string partition function.

  • Confusing the log de Rham complex with the ordinary de Rham complex; the log version includes logarithmic differentials along the divisor.
  • Assuming the log étale fundamental group is the same as the topological fundamental group of the Kato–Nakayama space without checking the fs condition on the log structure.
  • Neglecting the monodromy operator N in the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism; it is essential for matching the weight filtration.
  • Treating log prismatic cohomology as a mere variant of crystalline cohomology; the log Nygaard filtration and the log Breuil–Kisin classification are distinct new features.
  • Overlooking the role of the log structure on the Fargues–Fontaine curve when classifying vector bundles; the divisor at infinity carries the ramification data.
  • Applying ordinary motivic homotopy theory to log schemes without using log correspondences; the log Nisnevich topology is strictly finer.
  • Misidentifying the tropicalization map for a log smooth family; it lands in the cone complex, not in the usual tropical variety of the generic fiber.

hand/homotopy-type-theory.html:
Cubical Type Theory and Computational Univalence

Cubical type theory provides a constructive model of homotopy type theory in which the univalence axiom computes. Introduced by Cohen, Coquand, Huber, and Mörtberg in their 2016 paper Cubical Type Theory: a constructive interpretation of the univalence axiom, the theory extends Martin‑Löf type theory with an interval type I having endpoints 0 and 1. A path in a type A is a function I → A, and path composition, inversion, and higher coherences are expressed by Kan composition operations comp and hcomp. The crucial addition is the Glue type former, which internalises the equivalence‑to‑equality map and makes univalence a theorem rather than an axiom. As a consequence, closed terms of natural number type reduce to numerals — canonicity holds — and transport along ua(e) for an equivalence e reduces definitionally to the action of e. This computational behaviour is absent in the original axiomatic formulation, where transport is stuck at the axiom.

The first implementation was Cubical Agda (2019) by Vezzosi, Mörtberg, and Abel, which integrates cubical primitives directly into the Agda language. Subsequent work produced Cartesian cubical type theory (Angiuli, Favonia, Harper, 2021) to simplify universe management and support higher inductive types with computational rules. Cubical type theory also validates function extensionality and propositional extensionality by computation, and it has become the basis for several formalisation projects that require executable proofs, such as the verification of the Brunerie number in synthetic homotopy theory.

Higher Inductive‑Inductive Types and Quotients

Higher inductive‑inductive types (HIITs) generalise higher inductive types by allowing a type and a family over that type to be defined simultaneously. The concept was introduced by Altenkirch, Capriotti, and others in the 2017 paper Higher Inductive‑Inductive Types. A canonical example is the Cauchy real numbers: one defines a type ℝ of real numbers together with a family ≈ of approximation relations, with constructors for rational approximations, limits, and the required equalities. Another example is the syntax of dependent type theory itself, where contexts, types, and terms are defined mutually with their well‑formedness predicates.

Quotient types arise as a special case of HIITs. Given a type A and a relation R : A → A → 𝒰, the quotient A/R can be presented as a higher inductive type with a point constructor q : A → A/R and a path constructor eq : ∀ {x y}, R x y → q x = q y. When the quotient is required to be a set (0‑truncated), an additional truncation constructor is added. HIITs allow the relation R to be defined inductively at the same time as the quotient, which is essential for constructing quotients of higher structures such as the free group on a type or the set‑quotient of a groupoid. These constructions have been formalised in Cubical Agda and in the Coq HoTT library, and they admit an initial‑algebra semantics in any (∞,1)‑topos.

Worked Example: Defining the Integers as a HIIT
Show how the integers ℤ can be defined as a higher inductive‑inductive type with a simultaneous equivalence relation, and explain why this avoids the need for a separate set‑quotient construction.

Define a type ℤ and a family _≈_ : ℤ → ℤ → 𝒰 by the following constructors:

  • zero : ℤ
  • pos : ℕ → ℤ
  • neg : ℕ → ℤ
  • eq_pos_zero : pos 0 ≈ zero
  • eq_neg_zero : neg 0 ≈ zero
  • eq_pos_succ : ∀ n, pos (n+1) ≈ pos n
  • eq_neg_succ : ∀ n, neg (n+1) ≈ neg n
  • eq_pos_neg : ∀ n, pos n ≈ neg n (for n>0)

The relation ≈ is generated inductively by these constructors together with reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity (which are also constructors of the family). Because the equivalence relation is built simultaneously with the type, the resulting ℤ is already a set — no separate 0‑truncation is needed. The usual integer operations are then defined by recursion on the constructors, and the fact that they respect ≈ follows by induction on the relation. This pattern generalises to any quotient where the relation is inductively generated.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a quotient construction in HoTT, first decide whether the relation is decidable or inductively generated. If it is inductively generated, reach for a HIIT; if it is an arbitrary equivalence relation on a set, a plain HIT with a truncation constructor suffices. Remember that HIITs give you the quotient and its equivalence relation in one go, which often simplifies the proof that the quotient is a set.

Modalities and Cohesive Homotopy Type Theory

Modalities in HoTT are idempotent (co)monads on the universe that capture notions of “being of a certain shape”. The systematic study began with Shulman’s 2015 work Brouwer’s fixed‑point theorem in real‑cohesive homotopy type theory. A modality consists of an endofunctor ○ : 𝒰 → 𝒰 equipped with a unit η : A → ○A such that ○η and η○ are equivalences. Common modalities include n‑truncation (‖−‖ₙ), the double negation modality, and the shape modality ʃ.

Cohesive HoTT adds a string of adjoint modalities ʃ ⊣ ♭ ⊣ ♯ satisfying axioms that mirror Lawvere’s cohesion: ʃ (shape) preserves finite products, ♭ (flat) gives the discrete reflection, and ♯ (sharp) gives the codiscrete reflection. These modalities allow one to do synthetic differential geometry inside type theory: the real line ℝ can be equipped with a cohesive structure where ♭ℝ is the discrete real line and ʃℝ is its fundamental ∞‑groupoid. The axioms have been formalised in the RealCohesiveHoTT library for Coq and in Agda, and they enable the definition of differential cohomology, de Rham cohomology, and the synthetic formulation of the Stokes theorem.

Synthetic ∞‑Category Theory in HoTT

Because types in HoTT behave as ∞‑groupoids, the theory serves as a native language for (∞,1)‑categories. A precategory consists of a type of objects Ob and for each x y : Ob a hom‑type Hom(x,y) that is a set (1‑truncated), together with composition and identities. A univalent category (or complete Segal type) further requires that the canonical map Ob → Core(C) from objects to the core (the maximal subgroupoid) is an equivalence — this is precisely the Rezk completeness condition. Ahrens, Kapulkin, and Shulman (2015) proved that every precategory admits a Rezk completion into a univalent category, and that the type of univalent categories is itself a higher inductive type.

Higher categorical structures are encoded as Segal types: a type X equipped with maps Xₙ → X₁ ×X₀ … ×X₀ X₁ that are equivalences. Completeness (the Rezk condition) is again expressed by a univalence‑like axiom. These ideas have been formalised in the UniMath library (Coq) and in the Agda HoTT library, providing a foundation for (∞,1)‑topos theory and higher algebra inside proof assistants. The synthetic approach avoids the combinatorial complexity of simplicial models and makes the ∞‑categorical reasoning directly accessible to type‑theoretic computation.

Formalization of Algebraic Topology in Proof Assistants

The HoTT libraries in Coq (started 2014) and Agda (started 2015) have been used to formalise a substantial body of synthetic homotopy theory. Landmark results include the proof that π₁(S¹) = ℤ (Licata and Shulman, 2013) and the computation of the Brunerie number π₄(S³) = ℤ/2ℤ (Brunerie, 2016), the latter requiring a lengthy cubical computation that was later verified in Cubical Agda. The Blakers‑Massey theorem was formalised by Finster, Licata, and others (2018) in Agda, and the Serre spectral sequence was constructed by Buchholtz and Rijke (2020) in Agda, providing a powerful computational tool for higher homotopy groups.

Beyond homotopy theory, the UniMath project (Voevodsky et al.) formalises mathematics using univalence in Coq, including categories, homological algebra, and parts of algebraic geometry. In Lean, the mathlib community completed a formal proof of the Atiyah‑Singer index theorem (2023), demonstrating that HoTT‑inspired techniques can scale to deep analytic results. Cubical Agda’s computational univalence has been essential for verifying concrete numbers such as the Brunerie number, while the Coq HoTT library emphasises axiomatic development. Current challenges include universe management, performance of higher inductive type elimination, and automation of synthetic arguments, but the trajectory shows that machine‑checked proofs of major topological theorems are becoming routine.

  • Confusing the computational content of cubical univalence with the axiomatic univalence of Martin‑Löf type theory; the former reduces transport, the latter does not.
  • Assuming every quotient can be built as a plain HIT; quotients with inductively generated relations require HIITs.
  • Treating modalities as mere truncations; cohesive modalities have specific adjointness and product‑preservation axioms that are not satisfied by n‑truncation.
  • Believing that a precategory is automatically a category; Rezk completeness is an extra condition equivalent to univalence of the object type.
  • Thinking that formalised homotopy groups in HoTT are merely translations of classical proofs; many synthetic proofs (e.g., Blakers‑Massey) are genuinely new and simpler.
  • These traps highlight the most common misunderstandings in advanced HoTT topics.

hand/metallurgy.html:
Thermodynamic Constraints in Selective Reduction of Mixed Oxide Ores

When an ore contains two or more metal oxides, the Ellingham diagram alone does not guarantee selective reduction; the relative positions of the oxide formation lines must be examined together with the partial pressure of the reducing gas. For a mixture of Fe₂O₃ and MnO₂, the Fe₂O₃/Fe line lies above the MnO₂/Mn line up to approximately 1100 °C, meaning carbon can reduce Fe₂O₃ while MnO₂ remains stable. However, the reaction 2 C + O₂ → 2 CO has a steep negative slope; at temperatures above 1200 °C the CO line crosses the MnO₂ line, allowing simultaneous reduction of both oxides. In practice, a controlled atmosphere with a CO/CO₂ ratio fixed by the Boudouard equilibrium (2 CO ⇌ C + CO₂) is used to keep the oxygen partial pressure just below the Fe₂O₃/Fe equilibrium but above the MnO₂/Mn equilibrium. The equilibrium constant Kp for the reduction Fe₂O₃ + 3 CO → 2 Fe + 3 CO₂ is expressed as Kp = (pCO₂)³/(pCO)³; adjusting the gas composition shifts the reaction quotient Qp relative to Kp, enabling selective extraction. Similar principles apply to the separation of ZnO from PbO in the Imperial Smelting Process, where the ZnO/Zn line crosses the C/CO line near 950 °C, while PbO/Pb remains reducible at lower temperatures. The key thermodynamic parameters — ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° for each oxide formation — are tabulated in standard data books; the temperature at which ΔG° for the target oxide becomes less negative than that for the unwanted oxide defines the selectivity window.

Industrial practice exploits this window by staging the furnace: a high‑temperature zone (≈ 1300 °C) reduces the more stable oxide, while a lower‑temperature zone (≈ 900 °C) prevents reduction of the less stable oxide. The off‑gas composition is continuously monitored by zirconia oxygen sensors, and the carbon feed rate is modulated to maintain the desired CO/CO₂ ratio. Any deviation leads to either incomplete reduction of the target metal or contamination of the product with the undesired metal. The thermodynamic analysis is therefore coupled with real‑time gas analysis to achieve the required selectivity.

Kinetic Limitations and Process Control in Smelting Operations

Thermodynamic feasibility does not guarantee a practical rate; kinetic barriers such as solid‑state diffusion, nucleation of the metallic phase, and gas‑solid mass transfer often dominate smelting performance. In the blast furnace, the reduction of Fe₂O₃ to Fe proceeds through a series of intermediate oxides (Fe₃O₄, FeO) and the rate‑determining step shifts with temperature: below 900 °C the reduction of Fe₃O₄ to FeO by CO is controlled by chemical reaction at the oxide surface, while above 1000 °C the reduction of FeO to Fe becomes limited by carbon diffusion through the porous wüstite layer. The shrinking‑core model describes the conversion of a spherical ore particle: the reaction front moves inward, and the overall time for complete reduction t ∝ R²/Dₑ, where R is the particle radius and Dₑ the effective diffusivity of the reducing gas in the product layer. Consequently, fine ore (R ≈ 1 mm) reduces in minutes, whereas lump ore (R ≈ 10 mm) requires hours, dictating the burden size distribution in the furnace.

Mass‑transfer limitations also appear in the gas phase. The CO concentration at the particle surface is lower than in the bulk gas because of the consumption rate; the external mass‑transfer coefficient k₉ depends on the Reynolds number (Re) and Schmidt number (Sc) of the gas flow through the packed bed. Empirical correlations such as Sh = 2 + 0.6 Re⁰·⁵ Sc⁰·³³ (where Sh is the Sherwood number) are used to estimate k₉. Process control systems therefore regulate the blast velocity and temperature profile to keep Re in a range that maximizes k₉ without causing excessive pressure drop or channeling. Modern furnaces employ thermocouple arrays and off‑gas analyzers linked to a model‑predictive controller that adjusts the coke rate, oxygen enrichment, and burden distribution in real time, minimizing the deviation from the optimal kinetic regime.

Examiner's twist
A blast furnace operates at 1150 °C with a burden of hematite (Fe₂O₃) particles of 5 mm radius. The effective diffusivity of CO in the wüstite product layer is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹. Using the shrinking‑core model for diffusion‑controlled reduction, estimate the time required for 90 % conversion of a single particle. Assume the reaction stoichiometry FeO + CO → Fe + CO₂ and that the molar volume of FeO is 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹.
For diffusion control, the time for fractional conversion X is t = (R² / 6 Dₑ) [1 − 3(1 − X)²ᐟ³ + 2(1 − X)]. With X = 0.90, (1 − X) = 0.10. Compute (1 − X)²ᐟ³ = 0.10²ᐟ³ ≈ 0.215. Then bracket term = 1 − 3(0.215) + 2(0.10) = 1 − 0.645 + 0.20 = 0.555. R = 5 mm = 5 × 10⁻³ m. R² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m². Dₑ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹. t = (2.5 × 10⁻⁵ / (6 × 2 × 10⁻⁶)) × 0.555 = (2.5 × 10⁻⁵ / 1.2 × 10⁻⁵) × 0.555 ≈ 2.083 × 0.555 ≈ 1.16 s. The result shows that for a 5 mm particle at 1150 °C the diffusion‑controlled step is very fast; in practice the overall reduction time is dominated by the preceding chemical‑reaction steps and by heat‑up of the particle, giving typical residence times of several minutes.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for a kinetic estimate, identify the controlling regime (chemical reaction, diffusion through product layer, or external mass transfer) from the temperature and particle size given. Write the appropriate shrinking‑core or film‑diffusion equation, substitute the data, and keep units consistent. Examiners often award partial credit for correctly selecting the model even if the arithmetic contains a minor slip.

Electrochemical Extraction of Highly Reactive Metals: Hall‑Héroult and Downs Processes

Metals with very negative standard reduction potentials (e.g., Al³⁺/Al = −1.66 V, Na⁺/Na = −2.71 V) cannot be reduced by carbon at any practicable temperature; electrolysis of their molten salts is the only commercial route. The Hall‑Héroult process dissolves alumina (Al₂O₃) in a molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) bath at 950–970 °C. The overall cell reaction is 2 Al₂O₃ + 3 C → 4 Al + 3 CO₂, but the carbon anode is consumed by the oxygen evolved at the anode: 2 O²⁻ → O₂ + 4 e⁻; C + O₂ → CO₂. The theoretical decomposition voltage for Al₂O₃ at 960 °C is about 1.2 V, yet industrial cells operate at 4.2–4.5 V because of ohmic drops in the electrolyte (≈ 1.5 V), anode overpotential (≈ 0.5 V), and cathode overpotential (≈ 0.3 V). Current efficiencies of 90–95 % are typical; the remainder of the charge produces side reactions such as the formation of CF₄ and C₂F₆ (perfluorocarbons) which are potent greenhouse gases. Modern prebaked anode technology and point‑feeder alumina addition reduce the anode effect frequency, lowering perfluorocarbon emissions by > 90 % compared with older Söderberg cells.

The Downs cell produces sodium by electrolysing a molten mixture of NaCl (≈ 40 wt %) and CaCl₂ (≈ 60 wt %) at 580–600 °C. The eutectic lowers the melting point from 801 °C (pure NaCl) to ≈ 580 °C, reducing energy consumption and material corrosion. The cell reaction is 2 NaCl → 2 Na + Cl₂; the calcium chloride is inert but increases the conductivity of the melt. A steel cathode collects liquid sodium (density 0.97 g cm⁻³) which floats on the denser electrolyte (≈ 1.6 g cm⁻³) and is continuously withdrawn. The anode is a graphite cylinder that evolves chlorine gas, which is captured for downstream chemical synthesis. The cell voltage is 3.2–3.5 V, with a current efficiency of 85–90 %. Energy consumption is ≈ 2.5 MWh t⁻¹ Na, significantly lower than the 13–15 MWh t⁻¹ required for aluminium, reflecting the lower decomposition voltage and the lower operating temperature.

Both processes illustrate the interplay of thermodynamics (ΔG° = −nFE°), electrolyte design (melting point depression, conductivity), and electrode engineering (material stability, overpotential management). Advances such as inert anodes (e.g., cermet or doped SnO₂) for the Hall‑Héroult cell aim to eliminate carbon consumption and CO₂ emissions, but long‑term stability in the aggressive fluoride melt remains a research challenge.

Slag Chemistry, Flux Design, and Impurity Partitioning

Slag is not a waste product but a engineered liquid phase that controls impurity removal, protects the furnace lining, and influences metal quality. The basicity index B = (CaO + MgO) / (SiO₂ + Al₂O₃) (mass basis) is the primary design variable. In ironmaking, a basic slag (B ≈ 1.2–1.4) efficiently absorbs acidic gangue (SiO₂, Al₂O₃) and sulfur via the reaction FeS + CaO + C → CaS + Fe + CO. The sulfur partition ratio Lₛ = (%S in slag) / (%S in metal) increases with basicity and temperature; typical values are 50–100 at 1500 °C. Phosphorus removal requires a highly basic slag (B > 2.0) and an oxidizing potential (high FeO activity) to form stable calcium phosphate (Ca₃(PO₄)₂). However, excessive FeO raises the slag viscosity and accelerates refractory wear. The optimum FeO content is therefore balanced around 15–20 wt %.

In non‑ferrous smelting, such as copper converting, the slag is silica‑rich (acidic) to dissolve FeO and form fayalite (Fe₂SiO₄), which lowers the liquidus temperature and keeps the slag fluid at 1200–1250 °C. The copper loss to slag is governed by the equilibrium Cu₂O + Fe ⇌ 2 Cu + FeO; the distribution coefficient D_Cu = (%Cu in slag) / (%Cu in matte) decreases with increasing matte grade and lower oxygen partial pressure. Flux additions (limestone, quartz, borates) are calculated from mass‑balance models that target a desired slag composition window (e.g., 35–40 % SiO₂, 20–25 % FeO, 10–15 % CaO). Modern practice uses thermodynamic software (FactSage, Thermo‑Calc) to predict phase diagrams, liquidus temperatures, and activity coefficients, allowing the operator to simulate the effect of a flux change before implementation.

Trace impurity partitioning follows the same principles. For example, arsenic and antimony preferentially enter the slag as arsenates and antimonates under oxidizing conditions, while bismuth and lead tend to remain in the metal phase. The distribution ratios can be expressed as functions of oxygen potential (pO₂) and slag basicity, enabling selective removal by adjusting the blowing rate or adding oxidizing agents (e.g., Fe₂O₃). Understanding these relationships is essential for producing high‑purity metals without downstream refining steps.

Energy Efficiency and Environmental Mitigation in Modern Pyrometallurgy

Pyrometallurgical processes account for a large share of industrial CO₂ emissions; the iron and steel sector alone contributes ≈ 7 % of global anthropogenic CO₂. Energy efficiency improvements focus on three levers: (1) heat recovery from off‑gases, (2) substitution of carbon‑based reductants with hydrogen or electricity, and (3) process intensification through oxygen enrichment and pressure operation. In the blast furnace, top‑gas recycling (TGR) combined with CO₂ capture can reduce coke consumption by 15–20 %. The recycled gas is stripped of CO₂ (by amine scrubbing or pressure swing adsorption) and reheated before re‑injection, maintaining the required CO/CO₂ ratio while lowering the net carbon input. Pilot plants in Europe have demonstrated a 30 % reduction in specific CO₂ emissions (t CO₂ / t hot‑metal) using TGR‑BF coupled with carbon capture and storage (CCS).

Hydrogen‑based direct reduction (H₂‑DRI) replaces the carbon reductant with H₂, producing water instead of CO₂. The overall reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3 H₂ → 2 Fe + 3 H₂O is thermodynamically favorable above 570 °C (ΔG° < 0). The MIDREX‑H₂ and HYBRIT processes operate shaft furnaces at 800–900 °C with 100 % H₂, achieving > 95 % metallization. The main challenges are the high cost of green hydrogen (electrolysis powered by renewables) and the need for a water‑gas shift unit to manage the H₂O/H₂ ratio. Life‑cycle analyses indicate that if hydrogen is produced from wind or solar electricity, the specific CO₂ emission can drop below 0.5 t CO₂ / t steel, compared with 1.8–2.0 t CO₂ / t steel for the conventional blast furnace‑basic oxygen furnace route.

Electrolysis of iron oxide (electrowinning) is an emerging route that bypasses the high‑temperature reduction step entirely. Laboratory cells using a molten oxide electrolyte (e.g., CaO‑FeO‑Fe₂O₃) at 1600 °C have demonstrated current efficiencies of 80 % and energy consumption of ≈ 3.5 MWh t⁻¹ Fe. Scaling up requires inert anodes stable in the aggressive oxide melt and a cost‑competitive electricity supply. Meanwhile, waste‑heat recovery from slag granulation, off‑gas combustion, and stove heating can supply 30–40 % of the plant’s thermal demand, reducing fuel consumption. Integrated energy management systems that couple the steel plant with a combined‑cycle power plant or district‑heating network further improve the overall exergy efficiency.

Environmental mitigation also addresses non‑CO₂ pollutants: SO₂ from sulfide roasting is captured in contact‑process sulfuric acid plants; particulate matter is controlled by electrostatic precipitators and bag filters; and heavy‑metal emissions (Pb, Cd, Hg) are minimized by sealed furnace enclosures and wet scrubbers. Regulatory frameworks (e.g., EU Industrial Emissions Directive) set limit values that drive the adoption of best‑available techniques (BAT) across the sector.

  • Assuming that a lower Ellingham line always guarantees selective reduction without considering gas composition and kinetic barriers.
  • Neglecting the effect of particle size on diffusion‑controlled reduction time and using bulk thermodynamic data for fine‑ore kinetics.
  • Confusing the Hall‑Héroult cell voltage with the theoretical decomposition voltage and ignoring overpotential contributions.
  • Treating slag as a passive waste rather than an engineered phase; overlooking the basicity index and FeO activity in sulfur and phosphorus partitioning.
  • Equating hydrogen‑based direct reduction with zero emissions without accounting for the carbon intensity of hydrogen production.
  • Overlooking the role of anode effects in perfluorocarbon generation during aluminium electrolysis and their impact on greenhouse‑gas accounting.
  • Failing to apply mass‑balance and thermodynamic software for flux design, leading to sub‑optimal slag composition and metal loss.

hand/morse-theory.html:
Morse‑Bott Theory and Degenerate Critical Manifolds

Classical Morse theory requires non‑degenerate isolated critical points, i.e. the Hessian is invertible. Many natural functions — moment maps, height functions on symmetric spaces, the energy functional on loop spaces — have critical sets that are smooth submanifolds. Morse‑Bott theory, developed by Bott in the 1950s, extends the Morse lemma to this setting. If f : M → ℝ is smooth and C ⊂ M is a connected component of the critical set such that the Hessian is non‑degenerate in the normal directions to C, then C is a non‑degenerate critical manifold of index λ equal to the number of negative normal eigenvalues. A tubular neighbourhood of C is diffeomorphic to the normal bundle, and f takes the form f(c, v) = f(c) − ‖v⁻‖² + ‖v⁺‖² where v = v⁻ ⊕ v⁺ splits according to the negative and positive normal directions.

The Morse‑Bott inequalities replace the critical point counts by the Betti numbers of the critical manifolds. For a Morse‑Bott function with critical manifolds C₁,…,Cₖ of indices λ₁,…,λₖ, the Poincaré polynomial of M satisfies ∑i tλᵢ Pt(Cᵢ) = Pt(M) + (1+t) Q(t) with Q(t) a polynomial with non‑negative coefficients. This yields strong constraints on the topology of M; for example, the even‑dimensional complex projective space ℂPⁿ admits a perfect Morse‑Bott function with critical manifolds ℂP⁰, ℂP¹, …, ℂPⁿ of indices 0,2,…,2n, giving the well‑known cohomology ring.

Handle decompositions adapt naturally: a critical manifold of index λ yields a handle attachment of the form C × D^λ along its boundary C × Sλ−1. The attaching map is the inclusion of the sphere bundle of the negative normal bundle. Cancellation of handles now requires that the attaching sphere of a (λ+1)‑handle intersect the belt sphere of a λ‑handle transversely in a single point inside the critical manifold. The Whitney trick still works in high dimensions provided the critical manifolds are simply connected and the normal bundles satisfy appropriate triviality conditions.

Applications abound. The moment map for a Hamiltonian torus action on a symplectic manifold is a Morse‑Bott function; its critical manifolds are the fixed point components of the torus action. The Atiyah‑Bott‑Berline‑Vergne localisation formula computes integrals over the manifold by summing contributions from these critical manifolds. In gauge theory, the Yang‑Mills functional on the space of connections modulo gauge has critical manifolds corresponding to flat connections; Morse‑Bott theory underlies the construction of the Atiyah‑Floer conjecture relating instanton Floer homology to Lagrangian Floer homology.

Cerf Theory and the Classification of Morse Functions on High‑Dimensional Manifolds

While Morse functions are generic, the space of all Morse functions on a fixed manifold is not connected. Cerf theory, introduced by Jean Cerf in 1970, studies the stratification of the space of smooth functions by their singularity types. A generic one‑parameter family of functions fₜ : M → ℝ encounters only two types of non‑Morse events: a birth‑death of a cancelling pair of critical points of adjacent index (a Morse‑Bott singularity of type A₂) and a handle slide where the attaching sphere of a (λ+1)‑handle passes over the belt sphere of a λ‑handle. Cerf proved that for simply connected manifolds of dimension ≥ 5, any two Morse functions can be joined by a path that avoids worse singularities; the only obstructions are the Cerf diagrams recording the sequence of births, deaths, and handle slides.

The Cerf diagram is a planar graph whose vertices correspond to critical points and edges to gradient trajectories. A birth‑death creates or annihilates a pair of vertices connected by an edge; a handle slide corresponds to a Reidemeister‑type move on the diagram. The fundamental result is that the group of pseudo‑isotopies of a high‑dimensional manifold is isomorphic to the group of path components of the space of Morse functions modulo these moves. This leads to the pseudo‑isotopy theorem: for a simply connected manifold of dimension ≥ 6, every diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity is pseudo‑isotopic to the identity, and the space of such diffeomorphisms is connected.

Cerf theory also provides a combinatorial framework for the h‑cobordism theorem. The handle cancellation process in Smale’s proof can be viewed as a sequence of Cerf moves that simplify the Cerf diagram until no critical points remain. The Whitney trick guarantees that the necessary handle slides can be performed without creating new intersections. In dimension 4, Cerf theory breaks down because the Whitney trick fails; this is the root of the exotic smooth structures on ℝ⁴ and the difficulty of the smooth 4‑dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

Modern developments include the work of Igusa on the stability of Morse functions and the construction of the Cerf complex, a chain complex whose homology computes the homotopy groups of the diffeomorphism group. The Cerf complex has been used by Hatcher and Wagoner to study the algebraic K‑theory of spaces and by Galatius‑Randal‑Williams to prove homological stability for diffeomorphism groups of high‑dimensional manifolds.

Worked Example: Cerf Move on a Handle Diagram
Consider a 5‑dimensional cobordism with a Morse function having a single 2‑handle and a single 3‑handle whose attaching spheres intersect algebraically once but geometrically in three transverse points. Describe the Cerf moves needed to cancel the pair.
The three intersection points indicate that the attaching sphere of the 3‑handle wraps the belt sphere of the 2‑handle three times. First, perform a handle slide of the 3‑handle over itself (a Cerf move of type “handle slide”) to reduce the geometric intersection number by two, using the Whitney trick in the 4‑dimensional level set (dimension ≥ 5 ensures the Whitney disks are embedded). After the slide, the intersection number becomes one. Now the attaching sphere and belt sphere intersect in a single transverse point, so the pair forms a cancelling 2‑/3‑handle pair. A birth‑death move (the inverse of a cancellation) removes both critical points, leaving a Morse function with no critical points. The cobordism is therefore a product.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks to “simplify a handle decomposition”, always check whether the ambient dimension is ≥ 5 and the manifold is simply connected. If so, the Whitney trick is available and you can cancel any algebraically cancelling pair after at most one handle slide. In dimension 4, state explicitly that the Whitney trick fails and cancellation may be impossible.

Morse‑Smale Complexes and Gradient Flow Dynamics

A Morse function f on a closed Riemannian manifold (M, g) is called Morse‑Smale if the stable and unstable manifolds of its critical points intersect transversely. The gradient flow φₜ of −∇f then defines a finite‑dimensional dynamical system whose chain recurrent set consists exactly of the critical points. The Morse‑Smale complex is the chain complex generated by the critical points, graded by index, with differential ∂p = ∑q n(p,q) q where n(p,q) counts (with signs) the flow lines from p to q of index difference one. The homology of this complex is canonically isomorphic to the singular homology of M.

Transversality is a generic condition: for a fixed Morse function, a generic metric makes the pair Morse‑Smale. The compactified moduli spaces of flow lines are manifolds with corners; their boundaries correspond to broken trajectories, which give the relation ∂² = 0. The Morse‑Smale complex provides a concrete, finite‑dimensional model for the Floer complex in symplectic geometry, where the gradient flow is replaced by solutions of the Cauchy‑Riemann equation.

Morse‑Smale dynamics also yields the Conley index, a topological invariant of isolated invariant sets that generalises the Morse index. For an isolated invariant set S, the Conley index is the homotopy type of the quotient N/L where N is an isolating neighbourhood and L its exit set. When S consists of a single non‑degenerate critical point of index λ, the Conley index is the pointed sphere S^λ. The Conley index is robust under perturbations and extends Morse theory to non‑gradient flows and infinite‑dimensional settings.

Applications include the proof of the Arnold conjecture for surfaces via Morse‑Smale homology (by Floer), the construction of the Morse‑Novikov complex for closed 1‑forms, and the study of gradient‑like flows on manifolds with boundary where the flow is tangent to the boundary. In computational topology, discrete Morse theory (Forman) provides a combinatorial analogue that works on simplicial complexes and is used in persistent homology algorithms.

Witten’s Analytic Approach and Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics

In 1982 Edward Witten gave an analytic proof of the Morse inequalities by deforming the de Rham complex. Let f : M → ℝ be a Morse function. Define the deformed differential dₜ = e−tf d etf = d + t df∧ on differential forms. Its adjoint with respect to the L² metric is dₜ* = d* + t ι∇f. The deformed Laplacian Δₜ = dₜ dₜ* + dₜ* dₜ is a Schrödinger‑type operator Δₜ = Δ₀ + t ℒ + t² |∇f|², where ℒ is a zeroth‑order operator. As t → ∞, the low‑lying spectrum of Δₜ concentrates near the critical points of f. Near a critical point of index λ, after rescaling coordinates by √t, Δₜ approximates the harmonic oscillator on ℝⁿ with λ negative directions. The number of eigenvalues in [0, ε] for small ε equals the number of critical points of index λ, and the corresponding eigenforms are exponentially localised.

Witten’s construction is precisely the supersymmetric quantum mechanics of a particle on M with superpotential f. The supercharges are Q = dₜ and Q* = dₜ*; the Hamiltonian is H = Δₜ. The Witten index Tr(−1)^F e−βH equals the Euler characteristic of M and is independent of t. This physical interpretation explains why the Morse complex computes homology: the supersymmetric ground states correspond to harmonic forms, and the instanton trajectories between critical points are the gradient flow lines that define the differential.

The analytic approach yields strong results. The Helffer‑Sjöstrand theory gives precise asymptotics for the eigenvalues of Δₜ, leading to the “Morse inequalities with remainder” that bound the difference between critical point counts and Betti numbers by the number of small eigenvalues. In the semiclassical limit, the tunnelling between wells is governed by the Agmon distance, which coincides with the minimal action of gradient flow lines. This perspective underlies the rigorous construction of Floer homology via the heat flow method and the proof of the Atiyah‑Floer conjecture for certain 3‑manifolds.

Applications to Topological Quantum Field Theory and Heegaard Floer Homology

Morse theory on infinite‑dimensional spaces is the engine behind several topological quantum field theories (TQFTs). The Chern‑Simons functional on the space of connections over a 3‑manifold has critical points corresponding to flat connections; its gradient flow (with respect to the L² metric) is the anti‑self‑dual Yang‑Mills equation on the 4‑manifold M × ℝ. The resulting Floer homology groups are the instanton Floer homology of the 3‑manifold, which Atiyah conjectured to be isomorphic to the Lagrangian Floer homology of the moduli space of flat connections on a surface — the Atiyah‑Floer conjecture.

Heegaard Floer homology, introduced by Ozsváth and Szabó in 2001, is a Morse‑theoretic invariant of 3‑manifolds constructed from a Heegaard splitting. The data is a symmetric product Sym^g(Σ) of a genus‑g surface Σ, equipped with a symplectic form and a pair of Lagrangian tori 𝕋_α, 𝕋_β coming from the α‑ and β‑curves. The Floer homology of these Lagrangians in Sym^g(Σ) is the Heegaard Floer homology ĤF(Y). It satisfies a surgery exact triangle, detects the Thurston norm, and gives a combinatorial algorithm for computing the knot Floer homology of links in S³. The theory has been extended to 4‑manifolds (Ozsváth‑Szabó 4‑manifold invariants) and to contact geometry (the contact invariant).

Both instanton and Heegaard Floer homologies fit into the framework of a (3+1)‑dimensional TQFT: to a closed 3‑manifold they assign a graded vector space, to a 4‑dimensional cobordism a linear map, and they satisfy functoriality under gluing. The proof of functoriality uses Cerf theory on the space of metrics and perturbations to show that the maps are independent of choices up to chain homotopy. The resulting TQFTs have deep connections to gauge theory, symplectic geometry, and low‑dimensional topology, and they provide the most powerful tools for distinguishing smooth structures on 4‑manifolds.

  • Assuming every critical manifold is a Morse‑Bott manifold without checking normal non‑degeneracy.
  • Confusing the Cerf birth‑death move with a handle cancellation; the former creates a pair, the latter removes a cancelling pair.
  • Forgetting that the Whitney trick requires dimension ≥ 5 and simple connectivity; it fails in dimension 4.
  • Treating the Morse‑Smale complex as defined for any metric; transversality is a generic condition, not automatic.
  • Misapplying Witten’s deformation by ignoring the rescaling limit; the harmonic oscillator approximation only holds after scaling coordinates by √t.
  • Believing Heegaard Floer homology is defined for any Heegaard diagram without admissibility conditions on the diagram.
  • Overlooking that the Conley index is defined for isolated invariant sets, not for arbitrary compact sets.

hand/category-theory.html:
Higher Categories and ∞‑Categories

Ordinary categories capture composition of 1‑morphisms strictly. In many geometric and algebraic contexts one needs to keep track of higher homotopies between morphisms, leading to the notion of an n‑category where k‑morphisms exist for 0 ≤ k ≤ n and composition is associative and unital up to coherent higher equivalences. A strict n‑category requires all higher associativity and unit laws to hold on the nose; a weak n‑category (or bicategory for n = 2) replaces equalities by specified invertible higher cells satisfying coherence axioms. The most widely used model for ∞‑categories is the theory of quasicategories (also called ∞‑categories in the sense of Joyal and Lurie): a simplicial set satisfying the inner horn filling condition. In a quasicategory the 0‑simplices are objects, 1‑simplices are morphisms, and higher simplices encode composable strings together with chosen homotopies. The homotopy category of a quasicategory is obtained by identifying 1‑simplices that are connected by a 2‑simplex; this recovers an ordinary category. The homotopy hypothesis states that ∞‑groupoids (∞‑categories in which every morphism is invertible) model homotopy types of spaces. Model structures on simplicial sets (the Joyal model structure) and on complete Segal spaces provide equivalent frameworks. Higher categories appear naturally in derived algebraic geometry, topological quantum field theory, and the study of (∞,1)‑toposes.

Enriched Categories and Internal Hom

Let V be a monoidal category (with tensor product ⊗ and unit I). A V‑enriched category C consists of a class of objects and, for each pair X, Y, a hom‑object C(X, Y) in V, together with composition morphisms C(Y, Z) ⊗ C(X, Y) → C(X, Z) and identity morphisms I → C(X, X) satisfying the usual associativity and unit diagrams internal to V. When V = Set with cartesian product we recover ordinary categories. Important examples include categories enriched over Ab (pre‑additive categories), over Top (topological categories), over Cat (2‑categories), and over chain complexes (dg‑categories). If V is closed monoidal, i.e. the functor – ⊗ A has a right adjoint [A, –] (the internal hom), then a V‑enriched category C is tensored and cotensored when the functors C(X, –) and C(–, Y) have left and right adjoints respectively. The internal hom [A, B] in V plays the role of an object of morphisms; for instance in the category of chain complexes the internal hom is the complex of graded maps with differential (df)(x) = d(f(x)) – (–1)|f| f(dx). Enriched Yoneda lemma states that for a V‑functor F: C → V the object of natural transformations from the representable C(X, –) to F is isomorphic to F(X) in V. This generalises the ordinary Yoneda lemma and is the basis for weighted limits and colimits in enriched category theory.

Computing a Left Kan Extension along a Terminal Functor
Let C be the terminal category 1 (one object * and its identity). Let K: 1 → E be the unique functor picking an object e₀ in a small category E. Let D be a cocomplete category and F: 1 → D the functor selecting an object d ∈ D. Compute the left Kan extension Lan_K F: E → D and describe its value at an arbitrary object e ∈ E.
The left Kan extension is given pointwise by the colimit over the comma category (K ↓ e). Since K is the functor from the terminal category, (K ↓ e) is isomorphic to the slice category E/e whose objects are morphisms f: e' → e in E and whose morphisms are commutative triangles. The diagram (K ↓ e) → D sends every object to the constant object d (because F(*) = d) and every morphism to id_d. The colimit of a constant diagram at d indexed by a category I is the coproduct of copies of d indexed by the set of connected components of I. In a slice category E/e the connected components correspond to the set of morphisms into e modulo the equivalence generated by factorisation; when E is a poset this is simply the set of morphisms. Hence (Lan_K F)(e) ≅ ∐f: e' → e d, the coproduct in D of one copy of d for each morphism into e. The universal property of the Kan extension follows from the universal property of this coproduct.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a Kan extension, first identify the indexing functor K. If K is dense (e.g. the Yoneda embedding) the extension is uniquely determined by a colimit formula; write down the comma category explicitly and recognise whether the diagram is constant, representable, or a known shape. This reduces the computation to a familiar limit or colimit.

Topos Theory and Internal Logic

An elementary topos is a category E that has finite limits, is cartesian closed, and possesses a subobject classifier Ω — an object together with a monomorphism true: 1 → Ω such that every monomorphism m: A → X is the pullback of true along a unique classifying map χ_m: X → Ω. The existence of Ω makes the lattice of subobjects Sub(X) a Heyting algebra naturally in X; the internal logic of a topos is intuitionistic higher‑order logic. The power object P X is defined as Ω^X; its elements correspond to subobjects of X. The Mitchell‑Bénabou language allows one to write formulas with variables ranging over objects of E, using the internal connectives ∧, ∨, →, ∀, ∃ interpreted via the Heyting structure on subobject lattices. A geometric morphism f: F → E between toposes consists of an adjoint pair (f^*, f_*) with f^* left exact; it corresponds to a continuous map of the associated locales. Grothendieck toposes are categories of sheaves on a site; they are exactly the toposes that arise as categories of sheaves for a Grothendieck topology. The classifying topos of a geometric theory T is a topos Set[T] such that models of T in any topos E correspond to geometric morphisms E → Set[T]. This establishes a precise equivalence between syntax (geometric theories) and semantics (toposes).

Kan Extensions and Density

Given functors K: C → D and F: C → E with E cocomplete, the left Kan extension Lan_K F: D → E is a functor equipped with a universal natural transformation η: F → Lan_K F ∘ K. When it exists pointwise, its value at d ∈ D is the colimit of the composite (K ↓ d) → C → E, where (K ↓ d) is the comma category of objects c ∈ C equipped with a morphism Kc → d. Dually, the right Kan extension Ran_K F is defined by a limit over the comma category (d ↓ K). A functor K is dense if the canonical map colim(K ↓ d) Kc → d is an isomorphism for every d; equivalently, the Yoneda embedding y: C → [C^op, Set] is dense. The density theorem states that any functor F: C → E with E cocomplete is the left Kan extension of its restriction along a dense functor. In particular, every presheaf on C is a colimit of representables, which is the categorical expression of the fact that the Yoneda embedding is dense. Kan extensions also give a conceptual construction of adjoints: if K has a left adjoint L, then Lan_K F ≅ F ∘ L; if K has a right adjoint R, then Ran_K F ≅ F ∘ R.

Monoidal Categories and Coherence Theorems

A monoidal category (C, ⊗, I, α, λ, ρ) consists of a category C, a bifunctor ⊗: C × C → C, a unit object I, and natural isomorphisms αA,B,C: (A ⊗ B) ⊗ C → A ⊗ (B ⊗ C) (associator), λ_A: I ⊗ A → A (left unitor), ρ_A: A ⊗ I → A (right unitor) satisfying the pentagon and triangle axioms. Mac Lane’s coherence theorem asserts that any diagram built from α, λ, ρ and identities commutes; equivalently, every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict monoidal category where α, λ, ρ are identities. A braided monoidal category adds a natural isomorphism βA,B: A ⊗ B → B ⊗ A satisfying the hexagon axioms; if βB,A ∘ βA,B = id then the braiding is a symmetry and the category is symmetric monoidal. A monoidal category is closed when the functor – ⊗ A has a right adjoint [A, –] (internal hom); the adjunction yields a natural isomorphism C(A ⊗ B, C) ≅ C(A, [B, C]). In a symmetric closed monoidal category the internal hom inherits a monoidal structure making it a cartesian closed category when ⊗ is the cartesian product. Monoidal categories provide the categorical semantics for linear logic, for tensor products in representation theory, and for the composition of quantum processes in categorical quantum mechanics.

  • Confusing strict and weak higher categories — strict n‑categories are rare in nature; most examples (bicategories, quasicategories) are weak.
  • Assuming every enriched category is tensored or cotensored — these require the base V to be closed and the hom‑functors to have adjoints.
  • Treating the subobject classifier Ω as a truth‑value object in a classical sense — in a topos Ω is a Heyting algebra, not necessarily Boolean.
  • Misapplying the pointwise Kan extension formula when the comma category is not small — the colimit may not exist even if the target is cocomplete.
  • Believing Mac Lane’s coherence theorem eliminates all associators — it only guarantees that any two parallel composites of associators and unitors are equal, not that they are identities in the original category.
  • Overlooking the distinction between braided and symmetric monoidal categories — the hexagon axioms do not imply β² = id.
  • Using the Yoneda embedding as a dense functor without checking that the target category is cocomplete — density guarantees the colimit formula, but existence of the colimit still requires cocompleteness.

hand/acoustics.html:
Acoustic Impedance and Wave Transmission at Media Boundaries

Acoustic impedance Z of a medium is defined as the product of its density ρ and the speed of sound v in that medium, Z = ρ v. When a plane sound wave encounters a planar interface between two media of impedances Z₁ and Z₂, part of the wave is reflected and part is transmitted. The pressure reflection coefficient R and transmission coefficient T for normal incidence are given by R = (Z₂ − Z₁) / (Z₂ + Z₁) and T = 2 Z₂ / (Z₂ + Z₁). The intensity reflection and transmission coefficients are the squares of the pressure coefficients because intensity is proportional to pressure squared divided by impedance. A large impedance mismatch (for example, air to water, where Z_air ≈ 415 Pa·s/m and Z_water ≈ 1.48 × 10⁶ Pa·s/m) yields a reflection coefficient close to unity, explaining why most airborne sound is reflected at a water surface. In medical ultrasound, coupling gel is used to eliminate the air gap between the transducer and skin, reducing the impedance mismatch and allowing efficient transmission of acoustic energy into tissue. For oblique incidence, Snell’s law governs the angle of transmission: sin θ₁ / v₁ = sin θ₂ / v₂. When the incident angle exceeds the critical angle θ_c = arcsin(v₁ / v₂) (for v₂ > v₁), total internal reflection occurs and an evanescent wave penetrates the second medium. This principle underlies the design of acoustic lenses and the operation of phased‑array transducers that steer beams electronically by imposing progressive phase delays across array elements. The concept of specific acoustic impedance also extends to porous materials, where the complex impedance accounts for both resistive (viscous) and reactive (inertial) components, enabling the prediction of absorption coefficients from measurable flow resistivity and porosity.

Nonlinear Acoustics: Harmonic Generation and Shock Formation

In linear acoustics the wave equation assumes that pressure perturbations are infinitesimal relative to the ambient pressure, so the principle of superposition holds. Real media, however, exhibit nonlinearity because the local sound speed depends on the instantaneous particle velocity: c = c₀ + β u, where c₀ is the small‑signal sound speed, u is the particle velocity, and β = (γ + 1)/2 for an ideal gas (γ = ratio of specific heats). This dependence causes wave steepening: compressive parts of a waveform travel faster than rarefactive parts, leading to the formation of higher harmonics as the wave propagates. The distance required for a sinusoidal wave of initial amplitude p₀ to develop a shock front is the shock formation distance x_sh = c₀² / (β ω p₀ / ρ₀ c₀), where ω is the angular frequency and ρ₀ the ambient density. In medical imaging, the second harmonic generated by tissue nonlinearity is exploited in harmonic imaging: the transducer receives at twice the transmit frequency, improving lateral resolution and reducing clutter from reverberation. Nonlinear propagation also underlies parametric arrays, where two high‑frequency primary beams interact in a fluid to produce a low‑frequency difference‑frequency beam with a narrow directivity pattern, useful for underwater communication and sonar. The Burgers equation, ∂p/∂x + (β / ρ₀ c₀³) p ∂p/∂τ = (δ / 2 c₀³) ∂²p/∂τ², where τ = t − x/c₀ is retarded time and δ the diffusivity of sound, provides a one‑dimensional model that captures both steepening and thermoviscous absorption. Numerical solutions of the Burgers equation predict the evolution of the waveform into a sawtooth shape and the eventual balance between nonlinearity and absorption that determines the shock thickness.

Worked Example: Shock Formation Distance in Air
A 1 kHz sinusoidal sound wave in air at 20 °C has a pressure amplitude of 200 Pa. Estimate the distance from the source at which a shock front first appears. Use ρ₀ = 1.204 kg/m³, c₀ = 343 m/s, γ = 1.4.
First compute β = (γ + 1)/2 = 1.2. Angular frequency ω = 2π × 1000 = 6283 rad/s. The shock formation distance x_sh = c₀² / (β ω p₀ / (ρ₀ c₀)) = (343²) / (1.2 × 6283 × 200 / (1.204 × 343)). Evaluate denominator: 1.2 × 6283 × 200 = 1.508 × 10⁶. ρ₀ c₀ = 1.204 × 343 = 413.0. Ratio = 1.508 × 10⁶ / 413.0 ≈ 3652. Then x_sh = 117 649 / 3652 ≈ 32.2 m. Thus a shock would form roughly 32 m from the source under these idealised conditions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the shock formation distance, identify the given amplitude, frequency, and medium properties first. Write the formula x_sh = c₀² ρ₀ c₀ / (β ω p₀) to avoid unit errors. Remember that β = (γ+1)/2 for gases and β ≈ 3.5 for water. If the problem supplies intensity instead of pressure amplitude, convert using I = p₀² / (2 ρ₀ c₀). Practice a few numerical substitutions so the algebra becomes automatic under time pressure.

Underwater Acoustics and Sonar Equation Fundamentals

Sound propagation in the ocean is governed by the same wave equation as in air, but the environment introduces strong depth‑dependent sound‑speed profiles caused by temperature, salinity, and pressure variations. The sound‑speed profile c(z) creates refraction that bends ray paths toward regions of lower sound speed, forming the deep‑sound channel (SOFAR channel) where sound can travel thousands of kilometres with minimal loss. Transmission loss TL in the sonar equation is expressed as TL = 20 log₁₀(r) + α r + A, where r is range in metres, α the absorption coefficient in dB/m (strongly frequency dependent, roughly α ≈ 0.035 f² dB/km for f in kHz), and A accounts for scattering, boundary losses, and multipath effects. The active sonar equation for a target with target strength TS is SL − 2 TL + TS = NL − DI + DT, where SL is source level, NL noise level, DI directivity index of the receiver, and DT detection threshold. Passive sonar omits the 2 TL term because only one‑way propagation is involved. Ambient noise in the sea follows empirical curves: shipping noise dominates below 100 Hz, wind‑generated noise peaks around 1 kHz, and thermal noise rises above 10 kHz. The figure of merit FOM = SL − NL + DI − DT determines the maximum detection range for a given target strength. Modern sonars employ beamforming with hydrophone arrays to achieve high directivity index, and pulse compression (chirp waveforms) to increase range resolution without sacrificing signal‑to‑noise ratio. Understanding the interplay between absorption, spreading loss, and the sound‑speed profile is essential for predicting sonar performance in both shallow‑water and deep‑water scenarios.

Psychoacoustics: Loudness Perception, Masking, and Critical Bands

Human hearing does not respond linearly to sound intensity; the perceived loudness follows a power‑law relationship described by Stevens’ law: L ∝ I0.3 for moderate levels. The phon scale equalises loudness across frequencies by referencing a 1 kHz tone: a tone of frequency f at sound pressure level SPL has a loudness of N phons if it sounds as loud as a 1 kHz tone at N dB SPL. The sone scale provides a linear loudness measure: 1 sone = 40 phons, and doubling of loudness corresponds to a 10‑phon increase. Frequency selectivity of the basilar membrane is modelled by critical bands, each approximately 1 mm wide on the cochlea, corresponding to a bandwidth that increases with centre frequency (about 100 Hz below 500 Hz, roughly 1/3 octave above). Simultaneous masking occurs when a masker tone raises the threshold of a nearby signal tone within the same critical band; the masking pattern is asymmetric, with upward spread of masking being stronger than downward spread. Temporal masking includes forward masking (masker precedes signal by up to 200 ms) and backward masking (masker follows signal by a few ms). These phenomena are exploited in perceptual audio coding (MP3, AAC) where frequency components masked by louder neighbours are quantised coarsely or discarded, achieving high compression ratios with minimal perceptual loss. The equal‑loudness contours (ISO 226) show that the ear is most sensitive near 3–4 kHz, and that low‑frequency tones require substantially higher SPL to achieve the same loudness. Understanding critical‑band rate (Bark scale) and the excitation pattern on the basilar membrane is fundamental for designing auditory models, hearing‑aid algorithms, and noise‑assessment metrics such as the A‑weighted sound level, which approximates the 40‑phon contour.

Acoustic Metamaterials: Negative Modulus and Subwavelength Imaging

Acoustic metamaterials are engineered structures whose effective dynamic mass density ρ_eff(ω) and bulk modulus K_eff(ω) can become simultaneously negative over a finite frequency band, yielding a negative refractive index n = √(ρ_eff / K_eff). This is achieved by embedding resonant inclusions such as Helmholtz resonators (for negative modulus) and membranes or side‑loaded cavities (for negative density) in a host fluid. When both parameters are negative, the phase velocity opposes the direction of energy flow, enabling phenomena such as negative refraction, subwavelength focusing, and acoustic cloaking. A planar slab of double‑negative metamaterial can act as a superlens, reconstructing evanescent components of a source field and achieving resolution beyond the diffraction limit λ/2. Experimental demonstrations have used arrays of split‑tube resonators in air to achieve negative modulus near 1 kHz, and membranes with attached masses to produce negative density at low frequencies. The effective medium description is valid when the unit cell size is much smaller than the wavelength (typically a < λ/10). Losses inherent in the resonant elements limit the bandwidth and figure of merit; active compensation using piezoelectric shunts has been proposed to mitigate dissipation. Applications include acoustic imaging through aberrating layers, noise barriers with subwavelength thickness, and directional antennas for underwater communication. The design process relies on retrieval methods (S‑parameter inversion) to extract ρ_eff and K_eff from simulated or measured transmission and reflection coefficients.

  • Confusing acoustic impedance with characteristic impedance of a transmission line; they are analogous but have different units and physical contexts.
  • Assuming the shock formation distance formula applies unchanged to liquids; the nonlinearity parameter β differs significantly (≈3.5 for water).
  • Neglecting the frequency dependence of absorption α in the sonar equation; using a single α value across a wide band leads to large range errors.
  • Treating the phon and sone scales as interchangeable; they are related by a logarithmic‑linear conversion, not a simple proportionality.
  • Believing that negative refractive index requires both negative density and negative modulus simultaneously; a single negative parameter yields evanescent waves, not propagating negative‑index behaviour.
  • Overlooking the critical‑band concept when estimating masking thresholds; using a fixed bandwidth (e.g., 100 Hz) across all frequencies misrepresents auditory filtering.
  • Applying the inverse‑square law in a waveguide or shallow‑water environment where modal propagation and boundary interactions dominate spreading loss.

These advanced topics extend the core acoustics curriculum into areas that frequently appear in higher‑level physics and engineering examinations.

hand/graph-theory.html:
Graph Minors and the Robertson–Seymour Theorem

The Robertson–Seymour theorem, proved over a series of twenty papers from 1983 to 2004, states that the class of all finite graphs is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation. In concrete terms, for any infinite sequence of graphs G₁, G₂, … there exist indices i < j such that Gᵢ is a minor of Gⱼ. A minor is obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges, and contracting edges. This deep structural result has two immediate consequences that appear repeatedly in competitive examinations.

First, any minor‑closed family of graphs (a family closed under taking minors) can be characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. For planar graphs the forbidden set is {K₅, K₃,₃}; for graphs embeddable on the torus the set contains 16 241 graphs; for linklessly embeddable graphs the forbidden set is the seven Petersen‑family graphs. Examiners often ask: “Which of the following graphs is a forbidden minor for the class of graphs with treewidth at most two?” The answer is K₄, because treewidth ≤ 2 exactly excludes K₄ as a minor.

Second, the theorem yields an algorithmic meta‑theorem: for any fixed graph H, testing whether H is a minor of an input graph G can be done in cubic time O(|V(G)|³). Combined with the finite forbidden‑minor characterization, this gives polynomial‑time algorithms for every minor‑closed property. However, the constant hidden in the O‑notation depends astronomically on |V(H)|, so the result is primarily of theoretical interest. In practice, examiners test the conceptual implication: “If a graph property is minor‑closed, does there always exist a polynomial‑time recognition algorithm?” The correct answer is yes, by the Robertson–Seymour theorem, even though the algorithm may be impractical.

Key Points for Revision

  • Well‑quasi‑ordering ⇒ finite forbidden‑minor set for every minor‑closed class.
  • Planar graphs: forbidden minors K₅ and K₃,₃ (Kuratowski’s theorem is the special case).
  • Minor testing for fixed H is O(n³); the constant is non‑elementary in |V(H)|.
  • Applications: treewidth ≤ k ⇔ exclude a (k+2)‑clique minor; linkless embeddability ⇔ exclude Petersen family.

Spectral Graph Theory — Eigenvalues and Expansion

Spectral graph theory studies the eigenvalues of matrices associated with a graph, principally the adjacency matrix A and the Laplacian matrix L = D − A, where D is the diagonal degree matrix. For a d‑regular graph the adjacency eigenvalues lie in [−d, d]; the largest eigenvalue is d with eigenvector 1. The second largest eigenvalue λ₂ controls many combinatorial properties.

The Cheeger inequality links λ₂ to the edge expansion (conductance) h(G) = minS⊂V, 0<|S|≤|V|/2 |∂S| / (d|S|). For d‑regular graphs it states: (d − λ₂)/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2d(d − λ₂)). A small spectral gap d − λ₂ implies the existence of a sparse cut; a large gap certifies that the graph is an expander. Examiners frequently ask to bound the expansion of a given regular graph when λ₂ is known, or to deduce that a family of graphs with λ₂ ≤ d − ε forms an expander family.

Ramanujan graphs are d‑regular graphs whose non‑trivial eigenvalues satisfy |λ| ≤ 2√(d−1). They achieve the optimal spectral gap given by the Alon–Boppana bound: for any infinite family of d‑regular graphs, lim inf λ₂ ≥ 2√(d−1). Constructions by Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak and by Margulis provide explicit Ramanujan graphs for infinitely many degrees. In competitive exams, a typical question is: “Show that a 3‑regular Ramanujan graph has λ₂ ≤ 2√2 ≈ 2.828.” The answer follows directly from the definition.

The Laplacian eigenvalues 0 = μ₁ ≤ μ₂ ≤ … ≤ μₙ give an alternative expansion measure. The second Laplacian eigenvalue μ₂ (algebraic connectivity) satisfies μ₂ = d − λ₂ for regular graphs. The same Cheeger inequality can be written as μ₂/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2d μ₂). This formulation extends naturally to irregular graphs, where the normalized Laplacian ℒ = I − D⁻¹ᐟ² A D⁻¹ᐟ² is used.

Key Points for Revision

  • Adjacency eigenvalues of d‑regular graphs lie in [−d, d]; λ₁ = d.
  • Cheeger inequality: (d − λ₂)/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2d(d − λ₂)).
  • Ramanujan graphs: |λ| ≤ 2√(d−1) for all non‑trivial eigenvalues.
  • Alon–Boppana bound: lim inf λ₂ ≥ 2√(d−1) for any infinite d‑regular family.
  • Laplacian μ₂ = d − λ₂ (regular case); normalized Laplacian for irregular graphs.
Technique: Applying Cheeger Inequality to Bound Expansion
A 4‑regular graph on 100 vertices has second adjacency eigenvalue λ₂ = 2.5. Estimate the edge expansion h(G) using the Cheeger inequality.
For a d‑regular graph, Cheeger gives (d − λ₂)/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2d(d − λ₂)). Here d = 4, λ₂ = 2.5, so d − λ₂ = 1.5. Lower bound = 1.5/2 = 0.75. Upper bound = √(2·4·1.5) = √12 ≈ 3.464. Since h(G) ≤ 1 by definition (maximum possible cut fraction), the effective upper bound is 1. Thus 0.75 ≤ h(G) ≤ 1. The graph is a reasonably good expander.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorize the exact form of the Cheeger inequality for both adjacency and Laplacian spectra. When a problem gives λ₂ or μ₂, immediately write the two‑sided bound; the lower bound often yields a quick “expander” conclusion, while the upper bound is useful for proving non‑expansion. Also remember that Ramanujan graphs are the only explicit constructions achieving the Alon–Boppana limit — this fact appears in multiple‑choice questions about optimal spectral gap.

Graph Homomorphisms and the Chromatic Polynomial

A graph homomorphism from G to H is a vertex map φ: V(G) → V(H) such that every edge uv ∈ E(G) maps to an edge φ(u)φ(v) ∈ E(H). When H = Kₖ, a homomorphism is exactly a proper k‑coloring of G. The number of homomorphisms from G to Kₖ is a polynomial in k, called the chromatic polynomial P_G(k). It satisfies the deletion–contraction recurrence: for any edge e, P_G(k) = PG−e(k) − PG/e(k), with base cases PEₙ(k) = kⁿ for the edgeless graph on n vertices and PK₂(k) = k(k−1).

The chromatic polynomial encodes rich information. Its degree is |V(G)|, its leading coefficient is 1, and the coefficient of k|V|−1 is −|E(G)|. The roots of P_G(k) (chromatic roots) are algebraic integers; a famous theorem of Thomassen shows that chromatic roots are dense in the complex plane, but for real roots they are bounded above by the maximum degree plus one. The value P_G(−1) equals (−1)|V| times the number of acyclic orientations of G (Stanley’s theorem). Examiners often ask: “Compute PCₙ(k) for the cycle Cₙ.” Using deletion–contraction repeatedly yields PCₙ(k) = (k−1)ⁿ + (−1)ⁿ(k−1).

Graph homomorphisms generalize coloring. The homomorphism order (G → H) forms a lattice; the core of a graph is its minimal homomorphic image. Determining whether G → H exists is NP‑complete for general H (Hell–Nešetřil theorem), but polynomial for bipartite H. In parameterized complexity, the problem is fixed‑parameter tractable when parameterized by the treewidth of G, a direct application of Courcelle’s theorem.

Key Points for Revision

  • Chromatic polynomial P_G(k) counts proper k‑colorings; degree = |V|, leading coeff = 1.
  • Deletion–contraction: P_G = PG−e − PG/e.
  • Cycle formula: PCₙ(k) = (k−1)ⁿ + (−1)ⁿ(k−1).
  • Stanley: P_G(−1) = (−1)|V|·(# acyclic orientations).
  • Hell–Nešetřil: H‑coloring is NP‑complete unless H is bipartite or has a loop.

Treewidth, Parameterized Complexity, and Algorithmic Graph Minor Theory

Treewidth measures how close a graph is to a tree. A tree decomposition of G is a pair (T, {X_t}t∈V(T)) where T is a tree and each bag X_t ⊆ V(G) satisfies: (1) ∪_t X_t = V(G); (2) for every edge uv ∈ E(G) some bag contains both u and v; (3) for each vertex v, the bags containing v form a connected subtree of T. The width is max_t |X_t| − 1; the treewidth tw(G) is the minimum width over all decompositions. Trees have treewidth 1; cycles have treewidth 2; the k×k grid has treewidth k.

Robertson and Seymour proved that for every fixed k, the class of graphs with treewidth ≤ k is minor‑closed and characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors (the (k+2)‑clique is one of them). This yields a cubic‑time algorithm to test treewidth ≤ k, but the constant is huge. In practice, competitive exams focus on the algorithmic consequence: many NP‑hard problems become linear‑time solvable on graphs of bounded treewidth via dynamic programming on a tree decomposition. Courcelle’s theorem (1990) states that any graph property expressible in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₂) can be decided in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth. Examples: Hamiltonian cycle, 3‑coloring, dominating set, Steiner tree.

Parameterized complexity refines this picture. A problem is fixed‑parameter tractable (FPT) with parameter k if it can be solved in time f(k)·nO(1). Treewidth is a central parameter: many problems are FPT when parameterized by treewidth, but W[1]‑hard when parameterized by solution size (e.g., clique). The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) implies that no algorithm can solve 3‑SAT in 2o(n) time; this transfers to lower bounds for treewidth‑based algorithms, e.g., Hamiltonian cycle cannot be solved in 2o(tw)·nO(1) unless ETH fails.

Key Points for Revision

  • Treewidth definition via tree decomposition; width = max bag size − 1.
  • Forbidden minors for tw ≤ k include Kk+2; grid minor theorem: large treewidth ⇒ large grid minor.
  • Courcelle’s theorem: MSO₂ properties linear‑time on bounded treewidth.
  • Dynamic programming on tree decompositions yields O(2tw·n) algorithms for many problems.
  • ETH lower bounds: no 2o(tw)·nO(1) for Hamiltonian cycle, etc.

Graph Limits and Graphons — The Analytic View of Large Networks

The theory of dense graph limits, developed by Lovász, Szegedy, Borgs, Chayes, and Sós, provides an analytic framework for sequences of graphs whose edge density stays bounded away from zero. A graphon is a symmetric measurable function W: [0,1]² → [0,1]. Every finite graph G on n vertices corresponds to a step‑function graphon W_G obtained by partitioning [0,1] into n equal intervals and setting W_G(x,y) = 1 if the corresponding vertices are adjacent, 0 otherwise. The cut distance δ_□(W₁,W₂) = supS,T⊆[0,1] |∫S×T (W₁−W₂)| metrizes the space of graphons modulo measure‑preserving bijections.

A sequence of graphs (G_n) converges if the homomorphism densities t(F,G_n) = hom(F,G_n)/|V(G_n)||V(F)| converge for every fixed graph F. The limit object is a graphon W such that t(F,W) = lim t(F,G_n). This is the dense analogue of the Benjamini–Schramm local convergence for sparse graphs. The Szemerédi regularity lemma is equivalent to the statement that every graphon can be approximated in cut distance by a step function with a bounded number of steps.

Applications include property testing: a graph property is testable with constant queries iff it is characterized by a finite set of subgraph density constraints (Alon–Shapira). In extremal combinatorics, the limit framework yields analytic proofs of Turán‑type results; for example, the maximum edge density of a triangle‑free graph is 1/2, attained by the bipartite graphon W(x,y) = 1x≤1/2<y or y≤1/2<x</sub>. Examiners may ask: “What is the limit graphon of the sequence of complete bipartite graphs K⌊n/2⌋,⌈n/2⌉?” The answer is the bipartite graphon described above.

Key Points for Revision

  • Graphon: symmetric measurable W: [0,1]² → [0,1]; step functions represent finite graphs.
  • Cut distance δ_□ metrizes convergence; homomorphism densities t(F,G) converge ⇔ graphon limit exists.
  • Szemerédi regularity lemma ⇔ graphons approximable by bounded‑step functions.
  • Testable properties ⇔ finite subgraph density constraints (Alon–Shapira).
  • Triangle‑free extremal limit: bipartite graphon with density 1/2.
  • Confusing minor‑closed with subgraph‑closed; minor‑closed families have finite forbidden minors, subgraph‑closed families need not.
  • Assuming Cheeger inequality gives exact expansion; it only provides bounds, and the upper bound can be trivial (≤1).
  • Thinking chromatic polynomial roots are always integers; they are algebraic integers, often non‑real.
  • Believing Courcelle’s theorem gives practical algorithms; the hidden constant is non‑elementary in the formula size.
  • Treating graphons as only for dense graphs; sparse limits require different tools (local weak convergence).
  • Forgetting that the grid minor theorem is qualitative — the function relating treewidth to grid size is not polynomial.
  • Review these traps before the exam.
